title: Relational databases and when SQL is right
scopeHtml: Scope: when SQL fits, schema design and normalisation, primary keys at scale, connection pooling with numbers, scaling reads, safe migrations. Questions are still to be written.

notes.title: What a relational database gives you
notes.html:
A relational database stores data in tables (rows and columns), links tables with keys, and lets you ask questions in SQL while promising that your data stays correct. The big promises are: a fixed schema, joins, constraints (a foreign key cannot point to nothing), and transactions (covered in a later note).

Why it is the default choice: the data is usually relational anyway (users have orders, orders have items), the query planner figures out how to answer ad-hoc questions, and 40+ years of tooling exist. Postgres and MySQL on one good machine handle far more than most startups ever need.

Worked example. A 64-core, 256 GB Postgres box with NVMe disks can serve roughly 20,000 to 50,000 simple indexed reads per second and 5,000 to 15,000 transactional writes per second (very workload dependent; always benchmark). A shop with 5M orders a year, about 0.16 orders/s on average, is nowhere near the limit.

Industry examples. Instagram ran on Postgres for years and sharded it only when needed. Stripe runs its core ledger on sharded MongoDB-style infra but uses strong consistency guarantees everywhere money moves. Shopify ran a huge MySQL fleet sharded by shop ("pods"). Stack Overflow served billions of page views from a few SQL Server machines.

Everyday analogy. A well-organised filing cabinet with a librarian (the planner) who decides the fastest way to find your folder, and rules that stop anyone filing a page under a customer that does not exist.

Common interview traps.

  • Saying "SQL does not scale". Single-node SQL scales a lot; sharding it is the hard, late step.
  • Picking NoSQL "because scale" with no number to justify it.
  • Forgetting that the choice is partly about queries: if you do not know your access patterns yet, SQL is the safer bet.

notes.title: When SQL is the right choice
notes.html:
Choose SQL when you need correctness across several rows or tables, flexible queries, or you do not know the future queries yet. Typical fits: payments, orders, inventory, bookings, user accounts, anything with money or stock counts.

Choose something else when: the data is a giant append-only stream (use a log or wide-column store), you need sub-millisecond key lookups at millions of ops/s (key-value), or the data is truly a graph with deep traversals.

Need SQL fits? Why
Money transfer between two accounts Yes Multi-row ACID transaction
Ad-hoc reports and joins Yes Planner handles unknown queries
1M writes/s of sensor points Not alone Single-node write ceiling; use LSM/time-series
Session lookup by ID at 500k/s Overkill Redis is cheaper per op
Friends-of-friends depth 5 Poor Many self-joins explode

Decision gravity. Choosing the primary store is close to a one-way door: moving 2 TB of live data between engines takes months (dual writes, backfill, verification). Choosing SQL first and adding a cache or search index later is reversible, because those are derived copies.

Industry examples. Uber's early trip store was Postgres, later moved to a custom MySQL-based "Schemaless" layer when write scale and sharding needs grew. Airbnb, GitHub and Shopify all stay on MySQL with heavy sharding rather than leave SQL.

Everyday analogy. A spreadsheet with strict column rules is great for accounting. It is the wrong tool for a stream of 100,000 sensor readings a second.

Common interview traps.

  • Using SQL as a queue (polling SELECT ... WHERE status='NEW'); use a real queue or SKIP LOCKED carefully.
  • Storing large blobs (images) in rows; keep them in object storage and store the URL.

notes.title: Schema design basics and normalisation
notes.html:
Normalisation means storing each fact once. If a customer's address is copied into every order row, changing it means updating thousands of rows and risking inconsistencies. So you put customers in one table and reference them by ID.

The rules in plain words:

  • 1NF: every cell holds one value, no comma-separated lists.
  • 2NF: every non-key column depends on the whole key.
  • 3NF: non-key columns depend only on the key, not on each other.
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id         BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  email      TEXT NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  created_at TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE orders (
  id          BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
  customer_id BIGINT NOT NULL REFERENCES customers(id),
  total_cents BIGINT NOT NULL CHECK (total_cents >= 0),
  status      TEXT NOT NULL,
  created_at  TIMESTAMPTZ NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created ON orders (customer_id, created_at DESC);

Notes on choices: money as integer cents (never floats); TIMESTAMPTZ not local time; a foreign key index is not automatic in Postgres, you must create it yourself or deletes on the parent scan the child table.

Worked example. 10M orders, each with a duplicated 200-byte address: 2 GB wasted, plus an address change touching up to dozens of rows per customer. Normalised, the address is one 200-byte row.

Industry examples. Most OLTP systems at Stripe, Shopify and GitHub are normalised to 3NF in the core, with deliberate denormalised read tables for hot paths.

Everyday analogy. A contact book where each person is written once and the party invite list just points to names, rather than rewriting everyone's phone number on every invite.

Common interview traps.

  • Floats for money.
  • Storing arrays or JSON in a column and then needing to query inside it constantly.
  • Using natural keys (email) as primary keys, then needing to change them.

notes.title: Denormalisation and when to break the rules
notes.html:
Denormalisation means copying data on purpose to avoid a join on a hot read path. You trade write complexity and storage for read speed.

Good reasons: a feed query joins 5 tables at 20,000 QPS; a counter like likes_count is read far more often than it changes; reporting tables. Bad reason: "joins are slow" with no measurement. Postgres joins on indexed keys are fast; the cost is usually in missing indexes.

Techniques: store a summary column (orders.item_count), a materialised view refreshed on schedule, a read-model table updated by a consumer from an event stream, or a cache.

Worked example. Order list screen needs customer name + item count + total. Joining 3 tables for 25 rows costs about 3 ms; at 10,000 QPS that is 30 cores busy. A denormalised order_summary row read by primary key costs about 0.3 ms.

Decision gravity. Reversible if the denormalised copy is derived and can be rebuilt from the source. One-way and dangerous if the copy becomes the only truth.

Industry examples. Twitter timelines are precomputed (fan-out on write). Instagram stores counters denormalised. Shopify keeps denormalised aggregates for dashboards.

Everyday analogy. Writing the total on the receipt instead of making the cashier re-add the items every time someone asks.

Common interview traps.

  • Denormalising without a plan for keeping copies in sync (drift bugs).
  • Counter columns updated on every like causing a hot row lock; batch or shard counters.

notes.title: Primary keys at scale
notes.html:
The primary key choice decides insert speed, index size and whether you can shard later.

Key type Pros Cons
Auto-increment BIGINT Small (8 B), sequential, cache friendly Single-node generator, leaks counts, hard when sharding
UUID v4 (random) Generate anywhere, no coordination 16 B, random inserts fragment the B-tree, poor cache locality
UUID v7 / ULID (time-ordered) Anywhere + roughly sequential 16 B, clock-dependent
Snowflake-style 64-bit ID 64-bit, time-ordered, no central DB Needs worker ID assignment, clock handling

A Snowflake ID packs about 41 bits of milliseconds, 10 bits of machine ID and 12 bits of sequence: up to 4096 IDs per ms per machine.

| 1 sign | 41 bits timestamp ms | 10 bits worker | 12 bits sequence |

Why random UUIDs hurt: in a B-tree, each insert goes to a random leaf page. With a 100 GB index that does not fit in RAM, nearly every insert causes a disk read plus later page splits, wasting about 30 to 50 percent of space. Time-ordered keys always append to the rightmost leaf, which stays in memory.

Industry examples. Twitter invented Snowflake. Instagram generates 64-bit IDs inside Postgres with a shard ID, timestamp and per-shard sequence. Discord uses Snowflake-like IDs. Stripe uses prefixed random-ish string IDs (ch_...).

Decision gravity. One-way door. Changing the primary key after 1B rows means rewriting every table and every foreign key. Pick before launch.

Everyday analogy. Numbered tickets at a deli (sequential, easy to find) versus random raffle numbers scattered across a giant wall (hard to keep tidy).

Common interview traps.

  • Exposing sequential IDs publicly (enumeration attacks, business metric leak).
  • Random UUID primary key on a huge InnoDB table: InnoDB clusters rows by primary key, so it is worse there than in Postgres heap tables.
  • Using 32-bit INT: it overflows at about 2.1 billion rows; this is a classic production outage.

notes.title: Connection pooling with numbers
notes.html:
A database connection is expensive, so you keep a small pool and reuse it. In Postgres each connection is a separate OS process using roughly 5 to 10 MB of RAM (more with work_mem use), and performance falls when active connections far exceed CPU cores.

A rule of thumb from the HikariCP project: pool size = (core_count * 2) + effective_spindle_count. For an 8-core DB server with SSDs, a pool of about 17 active connections total is often best, which surprises people.

Worked example. 50 app pods, each with a pool of 20 = 1,000 connections to Postgres. Postgres max_connections default is 100; raising to 1,000 costs about 5 to 10 GB RAM and slows everything via context switches. Fix: PgBouncer in transaction mode with default_pool_size = 40, max_client_conn = 5000. The database sees 40 connections, the apps see 5,000.

Little's Law helps sizing: connections needed = throughput x average query time. At 2,000 queries/s with 5 ms each: 2000 x 0.005 = 10 busy connections. So a pool of 20 is plenty; 200 is waste.

# pgbouncer.ini
pool_mode = transaction
default_pool_size = 40
max_client_conn = 5000
server_idle_timeout = 600
# HikariCP via Spring
spring.datasource.hikari.maximum-pool-size: 20
spring.datasource.hikari.connection-timeout: 3000   # ms to wait for a connection
spring.datasource.hikari.max-lifetime: 1740000      # below DB/LB idle kill

Transaction-mode caveat: session features (prepared statements across transactions in older setups, SET, advisory locks, LISTEN) break because the next statement may run on a different server connection.

Incident pattern. Symptom: p99 latency jumps, app logs "timeout waiting for connection from pool", DB CPU low. Metrics: pool pending count rising, pg_stat_activity showing many idle in transaction. Cause: slow transactions holding connections or a leak.

Industry examples. Instagram, GitLab and many Rails shops use PgBouncer. AWS offers RDS Proxy for the same purpose, valuable with Lambda where thousands of short-lived functions would otherwise each open a connection.

Everyday analogy. A kitchen with 10 stoves and 200 cooks queueing; adding more cooks to the pile does not cook faster, it just makes the kitchen crowded.

Common interview traps.

  • Increasing pool size to fix slowness; it usually makes it worse.
  • Forgetting total connections = pods x pool size when autoscaling.
  • Holding a connection open while calling an external API.

notes.title: Indexes and query shape for scale
notes.html:
Most "SQL is slow" problems are missing or wrong indexes. An index is a sorted side structure that turns a full table scan (read 50M rows) into a lookup (read about 4 pages). Details are in the index notes; here the schema-level rules:

  • Index every foreign key and every column in frequent WHERE/ORDER BY.
  • Put equality columns first and range/sort columns last in composite indexes.
  • Use keyset pagination (WHERE id < :last ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 25) instead of OFFSET 1000000, which scans and discards a million rows.
  • Check with EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS).
-- Slow at depth: scans and throws away 1,000,000 rows
SELECT * FROM orders ORDER BY id DESC OFFSET 1000000 LIMIT 25;
-- Fast: seeks directly
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id < 9000000 ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 25;

Worked example. A table of 100M rows at 200 B is 20 GB. A full scan at 1 GB/s is 20 s. A B-tree with fan-out of about 300 has height 4, so lookup is about 4 page reads, around 1 ms when cached.

Everyday analogy. The index at the back of a textbook versus reading every page to find "photosynthesis".

Common interview traps.

  • Too many indexes: each one slows every write and eats RAM.
  • Functions on indexed columns (WHERE lower(email)=...) without an expression index.
  • SELECT * defeating covering indexes.

notes.title: Scaling reads: replicas, caches, partitioning
notes.html:
The order of moves for a growing SQL database: tune queries and indexes, scale up, add a cache, add read replicas, partition big tables, and only then shard.

  • Read replicas: copy the primary's WAL stream. Reads go to replicas. Costs: replication lag (typically milliseconds, can be seconds under load), so "read your own write" needs care (route a user's reads to the primary for a few seconds after a write).
  • Table partitioning (within one DB): split events by month so old partitions can be dropped instantly and queries prune to one partition. Postgres declarative partitioning; keep partitions at a sensible count (hundreds, not tens of thousands).
  • Sharding (across DBs): split rows by a key (user_id hash) over several servers. Cross-shard joins and transactions become hard or impossible.

Worked example. 20,000 read QPS, 500 write QPS. A primary handles 500 writes easily; add 3 replicas each doing about 7,000 reads/s. Then a Redis cache with 90 percent hit rate cuts DB reads to 2,000/s, so one replica would do.

Decision gravity. Replicas and caches are reversible. Sharding is a one-way door: the shard key (user_id vs tenant_id) bakes into every query. Choose a key that keeps most queries on one shard and spreads load evenly.

Industry examples. Instagram shards Postgres by user. Shopify shards MySQL per shop. Notion sharded Postgres into 32 then 96 logical shards in their public engineering write-up (confirm figures in their blog). Vitess (YouTube) and Citus provide sharding layers.

Everyday analogy. A library adding photocopies of popular books (replicas) before building a second library across town (shards).

Common interview traps.

  • Reading from a lagging replica right after a write.
  • Sharding by an attribute that makes one shard hot (celebrity user, one huge tenant).
  • Promising cross-shard ACID transactions for free.

notes.title: Migrations and operating a big table
notes.html:
Changing the schema on a table with 500M rows is an operational risk, not a typing task. An ALTER TABLE can take a lock that blocks all writes.

Safe pattern ("expand and contract"):

  1. Add the new nullable column (fast in modern Postgres, metadata only).
  2. Deploy code that writes both old and new.
  3. Backfill in batches of 1,000 to 10,000 rows with sleeps.
  4. Switch reads to the new column.
  5. Drop the old column later.
-- Postgres: build index without blocking writes
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_status_idx ON orders (status);
-- Add constraint without a long lock
ALTER TABLE orders ADD CONSTRAINT total_nonneg CHECK (total_cents >= 0) NOT VALID;
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT total_nonneg;

Incident pattern. Symptom: all writes hang right after a deploy. Metric: lock waits, pg_locks showing an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE request queued behind a long-running query, blocking everything behind it. Set lock_timeout = '3s' on migrations so they fail fast.

Industry examples. GitHub's gh-ost and Percona's pt-online-schema-change do online MySQL schema changes by copying into a shadow table; Postgres teams use pg_repack and careful concurrent operations.

Everyday analogy. Renovating a shop while customers keep shopping: you build the new shelf beside the old one and move stock over, rather than closing the doors.

Common interview traps.

  • Running ALTER inside a migration with no lock_timeout.
  • Backfilling with one giant UPDATE that bloats WAL and locks rows.
  • Dropping a column in the same release that stops using it (old pods still running).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html:
• SQL is the default store for anything needing multi-row correctness and flexible queries; one good node goes very far.
  • Normalise the source of truth; denormalise only derived read copies you can rebuild.
  • Primary key is a one-way door: prefer 64-bit time-ordered IDs; avoid random UUIDs on huge clustered tables; never use 32-bit counters for big tables.
  • Pool connections small: about cores x 2 per DB, use PgBouncer; total connections = pods x pool size; Little's Law sizes it.
  • Scale in order: indexes, scale up, cache, replicas (watch lag), partitioning, sharding last.
  • Migrate with expand and contract, CONCURRENTLY, batch backfills and lock_timeout.
